910.name: Taíno and Indigenous Peoples of Xaymaca
910.description: The indigenous settlement of Jamaica, from early Redware peoples through the flourishing Taíno communities who named the island Xaymaca ('land of wood and water') and developed villages across the island before European contact.

sub_clusters.name: Redware Peoples and Early Settlement
sub_clusters.description: The earliest known inhabitants of Jamaica, referred to as the Redware people (related to the Saladoid culture), who migrated from South America and established fishing and foraging communities along the coastline.

sub_clusters.name: Taíno Settlement and Cultural Development
sub_clusters.description: The Taíno (Arawak-speaking) people who established villages across Jamaica, cultivating cassava, maize, and sweet potatoes using advanced conuco methods. They organized into cacicazgos and gave the island its name Xaymaca. Population estimates at European contact range from 60,000 to over 100,000.
key_events: Taíno establish extensive village networks across Jamaica
Estimated 60,000–100,000+ Taíno inhabit Jamaica by the late 15th century

920.name: Spanish Colonial Period
920.description: From Columbus's arrival in 1494 through over 160 years of Spanish colonial rule, during which the Taíno population was decimated, African slavery was introduced, and Jamaica remained a relatively neglected Spanish possession until the English conquest.

sub_clusters.name: Columbus Arrival and Spanish Settlement
sub_clusters.description: Columbus reached Jamaica on May 5, 1494, during his second voyage, claiming it for Spain. Juan de Esquivel established the first Spanish settlement, Sevilla la Nueva (New Seville), in 1509. The Taíno were rapidly enslaved and annihilated by forced labor and disease. Spanish Town (Santiago de la Vega) became the capital around 1534.
key_events: Columbus arrives at Jamaica — May 5, 1494
Juan de Esquivel founds Sevilla la Nueva 1509
Capital moved to Santiago de la Vega (Spanish Town) c. 1534

sub_clusters.name: Spanish Neglect and Introduction of African Slavery
sub_clusters.description: With the Taíno population devastated, Spain imported enslaved Africans to work on ranches and small sugar estates. Jamaica remained a colonial backwater as Spanish attention focused on wealthier mainland possessions. Some enslaved people escaped to the mountainous interior, forming the earliest Maroon communities.

930.name: English Conquest and the Age of Piracy
930.description: The English capture of Jamaica under Cromwell's Western Design, the rise of Port Royal as the 'wickedest city on earth' and pirate capital of the Caribbean, and its dramatic destruction by earthquake in 1692.

sub_clusters.name: English Capture of Jamaica
sub_clusters.description: Admiral William Penn and General Robert Venables captured Jamaica from Spain in May 1655 as part of Cromwell's Western Design. Spain formally ceded the island in the Treaty of Madrid (1670). The fleeing Spanish freed their enslaved people, who joined Maroon communities in the Blue Mountains.
key_events: English forces capture Jamaica — May 1655
Treaty of Madrid — Spain formally cedes Jamaica to England 1670

sub_clusters.name: Port Royal and the Golden Age of Caribbean Piracy
sub_clusters.description: Port Royal became the unofficial pirate capital of the Caribbean, enriched by buccaneers like Henry Morgan who raided Spanish ships and settlements with English approval. Known as the 'wickedest city on earth' for its taverns and debauchery, it was destroyed by a catastrophic earthquake on June 7, 1692, sinking much of the city beneath the sea.
key_events: Henry Morgan sacks Panama City 1671
Port Royal earthquake — June 7, 1692 — two-thirds of the city sinks into the sea

930.name: Sugar, Slavery, and the Maroons
930.description: Jamaica's transformation into Britain's most valuable sugar colony, the massive importation of enslaved Africans, the brutal plantation system, and the sustained resistance of the Maroon communities culminating in the Maroon Wars and peace treaties.

sub_clusters.name: The Sugar Plantation Economy
sub_clusters.description: Jamaica became Britain's most profitable sugar colony. Over 600,000 enslaved Africans were imported during the 18th century alone, working under horrific conditions on over 700 sugar estates. The planter class — known as the plantocracy — wielded immense political power in London.

sub_clusters.name: The Maroon Wars and Peace Treaties
sub_clusters.description: The First Maroon War (1728–1739) ended with a treaty granting the Maroons of Accompong, Trelawny Town, and other settlements internal autonomy and land rights in exchange for returning runaway enslaved people. The Second Maroon War (1795–1796) saw the Trelawny Maroons deported to Nova Scotia and later Sierra Leone.
key_events: First Maroon War peace treaty — Captain Cudjoe and the British 1739
Second Maroon War — Trelawny Maroons deported 1796

sub_clusters.name: Enslaved Resistance and Afro-Jamaican Culture
sub_clusters.description: Beyond the Maroons, enslaved Jamaicans resisted through revolts (Tacky's Rebellion 1760 being the largest), sabotage, and cultural preservation. African-derived traditions in music, religion (Obeah, Myalism), dance, and language laid the foundations for modern Jamaican culture.
key_events: Tacky's Rebellion — largest enslaved uprising in the British Caribbean, 1760

940.name: Emancipation, Rebellion, and Crown Colony Rule
940.description: The abolition of the slave trade, the pivotal Baptist War rebellion, full emancipation, the tumultuous post-slavery transition, the Morant Bay Rebellion and its aftermath, and Jamaica's conversion to Crown Colony rule.

sub_clusters.name: Abolition Movement and the Baptist War
sub_clusters.description: The abolition of the slave trade in 1807 was followed by intensifying resistance. The Christmas Rebellion of 1831–1832 (the Baptist War or Sam Sharpe Rebellion), led by enslaved deacon Samuel Sharpe, was the largest slave uprising in the British West Indies and accelerated Parliament's decision to abolish slavery.
key_events: Sam Sharpe's Christmas Rebellion (Baptist War) — December 1831–January 1832
Emancipation Act — August 1, 1834 (full freedom August 1, 1838 after apprenticeship)

sub_clusters.name: Apprenticeship and Free Village Movement
sub_clusters.description: After the transitional apprenticeship period (1834–1838), freed people established 'free villages' organized by Baptist missionaries. However, the planter class maintained economic dominance and political control, and the formerly enslaved faced continued exploitation and poverty.

sub_clusters.name: Morant Bay Rebellion and Crown Colony Rule
sub_clusters.description: Paul Bogle led the Morant Bay Rebellion in October 1865, protesting injustice and poverty. Governor Edward Eyre brutally suppressed it, executing Bogle and George William Gordon. The Assembly voted to abolish itself, and Jamaica became a Crown Colony under direct British rule.
key_events: Morant Bay Rebellion — October 11, 1865
Paul Bogle and George William Gordon executed 1865
Jamaica becomes a Crown Colony 1866

950.name: Labour Movement, Marcus Garvey, and Self-Governance
950.description: The emergence of Jamaica's modern political identity through Marcus Garvey's Pan-African movement, the 1938 labour uprising, the formation of rival political parties, the rise of Rastafari, and the path to independence.

sub_clusters.name: Marcus Garvey and Pan-Africanism
sub_clusters.description: Marcus Mosiah Garvey, born in St. Ann's Bay, founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA) and became the most influential Pan-Africanist of the 20th century, advocating Black self-reliance, African repatriation, and racial pride. His ideas profoundly influenced Rastafari, the Civil Rights movement, and Black consciousness worldwide.
key_events: Garvey founds UNIA in Kingston 1914
UNIA grows to millions of members worldwide in the 1920s
Garvey declared first National Hero of Jamaica (posthumously) 1969

sub_clusters.name: 1938 Labour Uprising and the Birth of Party Politics
sub_clusters.description: The Frome Sugar Estate revolt of 1938 sparked island-wide labour unrest. Alexander Bustamante founded the Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) and Bustamante Industrial Trade Union, while his cousin Norman Manley founded the People's National Party (PNP) — establishing the two-party system that endures today. Universal adult suffrage was granted in 1944.

sub_clusters.name: The Rise of Rastafari
sub_clusters.description: The Rastafari movement emerged in 1930s Jamaica following the coronation of Ethiopian Emperor Haile Selassie I, drawing on Marcus Garvey's teachings and African-derived spiritual traditions. Despite persecution, Rastafari grew to become one of Jamaica's most significant cultural and spiritual exports.

sub_clusters.name: Path to Independence
sub_clusters.description: Jamaica gained internal self-governance in 1944, briefly joined the West Indies Federation (1958–1962), and after a referendum withdrew to pursue full independence, achieved on August 6, 1962, under Prime Minister Alexander Bustamante.
key_events: Universal adult suffrage and first elections 1944
Jamaica votes to leave the West Indies Federation 1961
Independence — August 6, 1962

960.name: Post-Independence Jamaica: Culture, Politics, and Global Impact
960.description: Independent Jamaica's journey through Michael Manley's democratic socialism, Cold War-era political violence, the global explosion of reggae and Bob Marley, the bauxite economy, and the challenges of the IMF structural adjustment era.

sub_clusters.name: Early Independence and the Bauxite Boom
sub_clusters.description: Under Bustamante and his JLP successors, Jamaica pursued industrialization through the bauxite/alumina industry, tourism development, and the 'Industrialization by Invitation' model. The country experienced significant economic growth but persistent inequality.

sub_clusters.name: Michael Manley, Democratic Socialism, and Political Violence
sub_clusters.description: Michael Manley's PNP government (1972–1980) pursued democratic socialism, bauxite levy reform, and closer ties with Cuba, provoking fierce opposition from the JLP under Edward Seaga, the United States, and the IMF. The 1970s–1980s were marked by intense political tribalism and garrison violence, particularly around the 1980 election that saw over 800 killed.
key_events: Manley introduces bauxite production levy 1974
Green Bay Massacre 1978
1980 election violence — over 800 killed

sub_clusters.name: Bob Marley, Reggae, and Jamaica's Global Cultural Impact
sub_clusters.description: Jamaica produced an outsized global cultural impact through ska, rocksteady, and reggae music. Bob Marley became a worldwide icon of resistance and spiritual consciousness. Jamaican culture — from dancehall to Patois to cuisine — achieved remarkable global reach for a small island nation.
key_events: Bob Marley's One Love Peace Concert — April 22, 1978
Death of Bob Marley — May 11, 1981

960.name: Contemporary Jamaica
960.description: 21st-century Jamaica navigating crime and violence challenges, economic reform, climate vulnerability, sporting excellence (Usain Bolt), and continued global cultural influence through dancehall, athletics, and diaspora communities.

sub_clusters.name: Crime, Garrison Politics, and the Tivoli Gardens Incursion
sub_clusters.description: Jamaica grappled with high rates of violent crime linked to garrison politics and the drug trade. The 2010 Tivoli Gardens security operation to extradite drug lord Christopher 'Dudus' Coke resulted in over 70 civilian deaths and prompted national soul-searching about garrison politics.
key_events: Tivoli Gardens incursion — May 2010, over 70 killed

sub_clusters.name: Sporting Excellence and Global Brand
sub_clusters.description: Jamaica cemented its reputation as a sprinting superpower through Usain Bolt, who set world records in the 100m and 200m at the 2008 and 2009 events and won eight Olympic gold medals, alongside Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce and Elaine Thompson-Herah. Athletics became integral to Jamaica's national identity and global brand.
key_events: Usain Bolt sets 100m world record of 9.58 seconds — Berlin 2009

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
